images.caption: Slightly lifted from the soil, here you can see the broken edge of a biological soil crust. The sandy soil surface is glued together by microorganisms which prevent erosion and benefit the soil in many ways. Soil crusts are especially important in arid areas because there is less plant cover and more "bare" soil in-between. Physical processes also contribute to crusting of the soil and that is evident here too (smaller clay particles at the top, from nearby claypan). This particular crust was found in Diamantina National Park, Australia, which receives around 200 mm rain per year. The strands hanging down are probably of microbial origin, either cyanobacteria or fungi, and they reveal part of the internal crust structure which is tightly bound together with microbial filaments and sticky polysaccharide exudate. Most biological soil crusts are photosynthetic like plants, and sometimes they will turn green after wetting.

images.filename: Diamantina National Park, Astrebia Downs National Park in Australia (MODIS 2017-11-03).jpg
images.caption:
The rolling red grasslands of Queensland form part of the “outback” - a term that designates the remote open spaces of interior of Australia, where the skies are large, the rocks are red, and summers are hot and dry. In Central West Queensland the land is particularly rugged, especially in the Channel Country, a land notable for numerous intertwined rivulets which bring life-sustaining water to the region. The dramatic scenery combined with the presence of water creates the perfect setting for numerous parks which welcome hardy, well-equipped visitors with four-wheel-drive vehicles, as well as provide homes and migration stops for hundreds of species of wild creatures, including birds, mammals, marsupials, and more.
At times, visitors stay too long, and become a problem for the natives. Such a drama has been playing out in Astrebla Downs National Park. This very remote park was once home to a vigorous population of about 700 bilbies, which is the only free-ranging population of the cat-sized, long-nosed, gray-furred marsupial remaining in Queensland. Once wide-ranging across the interior of Australia, the bilby (Macrotis lagotis) has been in furious decline. It is listed as a Vulnerable species by the ICUN Redlist of Threatened Species, and has been extirpated in several parts of its native range across Australia.
The grasslands of Astrebla Downs make a fine home for the bilby – and also for a species known as the long haired rat. The rat population boomed in Astrebla Downs in 2009, and the resulting food competition began to erode the bilby population. On the other hand, the local feral cats enjoyed a huge boom as they feasted on easily-caught rat. When the rat population crashed in 2013, the cats turned to the bilby – and in a big way. An article in ABC News published in October 2014 reported only about 200 bilbies remained in Astrebla Downs. Vigorous control of the feral cat population is integral in restoring the bilby population in Queensland, as well as protecting native wildlife across Australia.
The Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) aboard NASA’s Terra satellite acquired a true-color image of part of the Channel Country of Queensland on October 30, 2017. Astrebla Downs National Park sits in the southwest corner of the image, marked by crescent-shaped wetlands and braided rivulets. To the northeast lies Diamantina National Park which sits along the winding Diamantina River.

Together, the two parks are part of the Diamantina and Astrebla Grasslands, which has been identified by BirdLife International as an Important Bird Area (IBA). It is home to the critically endangered night parrot, as well as globally important populations of many other species of bird.

images.caption:
On September 25, 2018, NASA’s Terra satellite flew over the rolling red grasslands and hills of Queensland’s “outback” – a term that designates the remote open spaces of Australia’s interior, where skies are large, the rocks are red, and summers are hot and dry. The Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) aboard that satellite acquired a stunning true-color image centered on Diamantina National Park on that same day.
The outback of South West Queensland, the home of Diamantina National Park, is particularly remote and rugged. Located roughly 250 miles (400 km) southeast of the town of Winton, the road to Diamantina, according to the Queensland Parks and Forests website, include at least 124 mi (200 km) of unsealed roads. They specify, “Road conditions vary but you will experience deep wheel ruts and areas of bulldust. Small amounts of rain can make the roads impassable.” And, “Not all roads and tracks shown on commercially-available maps, including GPS maps, actually exist and those that do may not be open to the public.”

The braided Diamantina River is the heart of the park and rises in the Swords Range (mountains) southwest of Winton. Although an ephemeral river – one that dries up in places in hot, dry summers – the Diamantina has been an important river for indigenous people, who used its shallow channels as a trading route, and a source for subsistence in the surrounding grasslands, sand dunes, and sandstone mountains. More recently the Diamantina’s grassland have been used for pastureland for livestock. Almost all of the land in the region outside of Diamantina National Park is currently being used for pasturage.
